stories.headline: Dolphins cut kicker Zane Gonzalez a day after costly misses in loss to Colts
stories.summary: The Dolphins waived kicker Zane Gonzalez on Monday, a day after he missed two field goals and an extra point in a 24-22 loss to the Colts.
stories.body:
The Miami Dolphins waived kicker Zane Gonzalez on Monday, a day after he missed two field goals and an extra point in a 24-22 loss to the Indianapolis Colts.

Dolphins coach Jeff Hafley expressed his displeasure with the missed chances at points on Sunday.

"We got to make the extra point, and we got to make the field goals," Hafley told reporters. "I'm not going to ever B.S. you. It's 24-22. A missed extra point forces us to go for two, and we missed two field goals. That's seven points. We have to make those."

The Dolphins currently don't have a kicker on their practice squad so they will have to sign a kicker this week. Miami worked out veteran kicker Daniel Carlson last week.

Gonzalez made six of his 10 field goal attempts in four games for the Dolphins since signing with the team last month. He had replaced Riley Patterson, who has since signed with the Baltimore Ravens.

The Dolphins are 1-8 in Hafley's first season as head coach.

stories.headline: NBA transaction glossary: Trade, free agency, extension, CBA terms to know
stories.summary: The world of NBA transactions is often difficult to decipher. Our resident GM is here to help.﻿
stories.body:
The world of NBA transactions -- with its two aprons, trade exceptions, Bird rights and all -- is often difficult to decipher. We're here to help.

From the basics of the league's collective bargaining agreement to the finest details of the salary cap, let's run through the most important terms you'll see on ESPN during the run-up to the trade deadline, the draft and free agency.

Jump to a section:

Basics | Roster rules | Salary cap and taxes

Apron | Free agency | Cap, trade exceptions

Extension types | Two-way, 10-day contracts

The basics
Collective bargaining agreement (CBA): A legal contract between the NBA and the National Basketball Players Association (NBPA), covering various aspects of league operations, including player salaries, revenue sharing and the salary cap. The current CBA was ratified ahead of the 2023-24 season and expired after the 2029-30 campaign. (Either side can opt out of the agreement for the 2029-30 season if written notice is provided by Oct. 15, 2028.)

Salary cap: The leaguewide limit on total player salaries ($165.0 million for 2026-27). Teams over the salary cap can add players only through exceptions or trades that match outgoing money.

Luxury tax: A higher threshold above the salary cap ($200.4 million for 2026-27). Teams in the luxury tax face penalties on every dollar above the line and have a smaller midlevel exception.

Aprons: Thresholds above the luxury tax line that trigger additional restrictions on team spending and roster-building. First apron for 2026-27: $209 million. Second apron for 2026-27: $221.7 million

Salary cap exceptions: Rules allowing teams to exceed the salary cap in specific scenarios, such as re-signing players with "Bird rights" or signing new players using the midlevel, biannual and minimum exceptions.

Trade exceptions: Created when a team trades a player. For teams under the aprons, the expanded traded player exception can bring in more salary than is sent out. For example, if Team A trades a player earning $14 million to Team B for a player earning $6 million, Team A will create an $8 million trade exception.

If a team acquires a player for a lesser salary than what is sent out, it unlocks the standard traded player exception -- used to acquire a player within a year, earning up to $250,000 more than the exception. Sign-and-trade: A contract mechanism in which players sign with their current team and are immediately traded. This requires a minimum three-year contract, with the first year guaranteed.

Teams above the aprons cannot acquire a player via sign-and-trade, and teams above the second apron can send out a player via sign-and-trade but cannot use that outgoing salary to bring back any in return.

Veteran minimum contracts: One- or two-year contracts based on a scale issued annually on June 30 by the NBA. If a player signs for one year at the minimum and has more than two years of service, their higher salary is treated as if they had signed as a veteran with two years of service (while receiving their full salary). An undrafted player with one year of service or fewer is counted as a veteran with two years of service against a team's luxury tax and apron salaries.

Two-way contracts: Players with three or fewer years of service are allowed to split time between the NBA and their team's G League affiliate. If signed before the regular season, the maximum allowable games is 50. A player is not eligible for the postseason. Players can sign up to three two-way contracts with their current team.

Roster rules

Offseason roster limit: During the NBA offseason (July 1 through Oct. 19), teams can expand their roster to 21 players: 18 standard contracts and three two-way contracts.

Regular season roster limit: During the regular season, teams can roster a maximum of 15 standard contracts and three two-way contracts.

Active list: The list of players eligible to play in a game, capped at 15 players during the regular season. Adjusted from previous CBAs, this rule increases flexibility, mainly when teams deal with injuries or suspensions.

Flexibility rules: Allow teams to have fewer than 14 players on standard contracts for a total of 28 days during the regular season. This can help teams manage luxury taxes and hard-cap costs, but they cannot go below 14 players for more than 14 consecutive days.

Full salary protection date: Though all non-guaranteed NBA contracts guarantee as of Jan. 10, the last day to waive a player without guaranteeing their full salary is Jan. 7 (5 p.m. ET). Players waived after this date receive their full salary for the season.

Hardship exception: Teams may gain an extra roster spot if four players are injured, with each missing at least three consecutive games (and all are expected to miss at least an additional two weeks). This allows a team to sign a player to a 10-day contract before Jan. 5. A team must have a roster spot available to sign a player to a hardship exception.

Playoff eligibility deadline: If a team requests waivers on a player by 11:59 p.m. on March 1, that player will be playoff-eligible upon signing with another franchise. A player who signs a 10-day contract that expires after March 1 is also playoff-eligible because that player does not go through waivers.

Voluntary retirement list: A list for players who retire before their contract ends; both the player and team must notify the NBA commissioner in writing. The player cannot return to the league for one year without the unanimous consent of the board of governors. If they wish to return, their rights go through the waiver process if their former team declines to re-sign them.

Salary cap deep dive

Cap increase limit: The maximum annual salary cap increase is 10%, and the limit cannot decrease from the previous league year. Cap increases since 2023-24, the first season of the current CBA:

2023-24: $136M
2024-25: $140.6M
2025-26: $154.6M
2026-27: $165M

Cap holds: Placeholder salary amounts assigned to a team's salary cap for various roster scenarios, such as veteran free agent holds, unsigned first-round picks or players with incomplete contracts. Cap holds affect how much salary space a team has to sign new players and prevent teams from using excessive cap space to sign new players without first addressing their own free agents.

Cap removal (for injured players): A team may apply to remove a player's salary from the cap in the event of a career-ending injury. If approved, salary removal can take effect one year after the player's final game.

Over-38 rule: This rule, originally introduced in 1995 as the Over-35 rule, closes a loophole where teams can sign aging veteran free agents to four- or five-year contracts. Some recent examples:

LeBron James, 41 (full Bird rights): At 41, James was eligible to sign for a maximum of three seasons before agreeing to a two-year contract with the Philadelphia 76ers this past summer.
Draymond Green, 36 (full Bird rights): After declining his $27.6 million player option to give the Golden State Warriors the salary cap flexibility to chase James, Green returned on a one-year, 27.7 million deal. His next contract cannot exceed three seasons.
James Harden, 37 (without full Bird rights): After declining his 42.3 million player option this past summer, Harden signed a three-year, $97 million contract to return to the Cleveland Cavaliers.

Stretch provision: If a player's remaining salary is above $500,000, a team can waive him before Aug. 29 and stretch the salary over additional years (the amount owed divided by two, multiplied by the number of years remaining, plus one). For example, Damian Lillard had two years and $112.6 million remaining on his contract. The salary owed was stretched over five seasons (two years remaining, multiplied by two, plus one). The Bucks' cap hit was $22.5 million over five seasons. If waived before Aug. 29, the player's salary is automatically stretched, but teams can choose not to stretch it against the salary cap.

Waivers: A process where a team releases a player from the roster, making them available to the league's other 29 teams for 48 hours. If the player is not claimed, they become a free agent and their remaining salary might still count against the team's cap unless a stretch provision is applied.

Supermax contract/extension: A contract or extension for players who meet specific performance criteria, such as All-NBA selections and Most Valuable Player and Defensive Player of the Year awards, allowing them to earn more than the contract limit. The extension allows for salary starting at up to 35% of the salary cap for six years (including the pre-extension seasons).

A player must have seven or eight years of service at the time the extension is signed. For example, Oklahoma City Thunder guard Shai Gilgeous-Alexander reached supermax criteria but was not allowed to sign until the following year, when he reached seven years of service. (A rookie-scale extension, similar to the supermax for players who reach the same criteria, tops out at 30% of the salary cap.)

Contract percentage increase: For a player with early and Bird rights, the maximum a contract can increase is 8%. For a player signed using cap space, an exception or via non-Bird rights is 5%. Raises are not compounded each season; for a player signed using cap space with a first-year salary of $20 million, the maximum in Year 2 is $21 million and in Year 3 is $22 million.

Luxury tax: A punitive threshold that penalizes teams for heavy spending. This is not a hard cap; teams are allowed to exceed the threshold. The penalties become harsher for repeater tax teams -- franchises in the luxury tax four consecutive seasons or four out of five seasons.

Luxury tax brackets: The tax brackets increase with the growth of the salary cap. The amount a team is penalized depends on whether a team is a standard tax penalty team or repeater.

2026-27 Standard tax penalties

Over tax by $1 to $6,063,999: $1.00-for-$1
$6,064,000 to $12,127,999: $1.25-for-$1
$12,128,000 to $18,191,999: $3.50-for-$1
$18,192,000 to $24,255,999: $4.75-for-$1
$24,256,000 to $30,319,999: $5.25-for-$1
$30,320,000 to $36,383,999: $5.75-for-$1
$36,384,000 to $42,447,999: $6.25-for-$1

2026-27 Repeater tax penalties

Over tax by $1 to $6,063,999: $3.00-for-$1
$6,064,000 to $12,127,999: $3.25-for-$1
$12,128,000 to $18,191,999: $5.50-for-$1
$18,192,000 to $24,255,999: $6.75-for-$1
$24,256,000 to $30,319,999: $7.25-for-$1
$30,320,000 to $36,383,999: $7.75-for-$1
$36,384,000 to $42,447,999: $8.25-for-$1

Note: Deeper brackets increase by $0.50. For example, being $42,448,000 to $48,511,999 over the tax results in a $6.75-for-$1 penalty ($8.75-for-$1 penalty for repeater teams).

Luxury tax distribution: Half of luxury taxes collected are sent to the teams below the tax threshold. Teams that fail to meet the salary floor by the start of the season will lose eligibility to receive this distribution.

Taxable salaries and bonuses

Incentives: Performance bonuses that count toward teams' luxury tax if earned during the season. An unlikely bonus counts toward the first and second apron. A player's salary can change during the regular or offseason if they had an unlikely/likely bonus. For example, Dillon Brooks had a $1 million likely bonus for Houston reaching the first round of the playoffs. Brooks was traded to Phoenix, and the bonus was deemed unlikely.

Trade bonuses: Bonuses received by players upon being traded. A trade bonus cannot exceed the maximum salary allowed. The bonus is a percentage (not exceeding 15%) of the salary owed. For example, if a player is owed 15% of his $20 million owed salary at the time of being traded (before the season starts), then he will earn $3 million. The bonus is added to the salary and counts as incoming salary. For a player with two-plus years on their contract, the bonus is spread evenly over years left unless there is a player option in the last year.

Suspension deductions: A portion (50%) of any salary lost due to suspension is credited as a tax variance, reducing the tax liability. For example, Paul George was suspended 25 games last season by the NBA. There was a $5,871,147 tax variance credit (50% of the suspended amount) applied to the 76ers' team salary that applied toward the luxury tax (not to either apron).

10-Day Contracts and Minimum Salaries: Undrafted players with zero or one year of service on minimum contracts count toward the team's tax payroll as if they had two years of service.

The aprons
Hard cap: A fixed salary cap limit that teams cannot exceed for the rest of the season, usually triggered by certain actions, such as using specific exceptions or acquiring players in a sign-and-trade.

Taxpayer midlevel exception: A spending tool that allows teams above the salary cap but below the second apron to sign a player for a fixed amount. This exception becomes unusable by teams exceeding the second apron. A team is hard-capped at the second apron if the exception is used. Example: Phoenix signed Luke Kennard to the tax midlevel exception.

Non-taxpayer midlevel and biannual exception: An exception for teams below the first apron to sign a player without exceeding cap space, with a value higher than the Taxpayer Midlevel Exception. A team is hard-capped at the first apron if either exception is used. Example: Boston signed Mitchell Robinson to the non-tax midlevel exception. The Pacers signed Kelly Oubre to more than $6.06 million of the non-tax midlevel exception and, as a result, are hard-capped at the first apron.

Sign-and-trade: A team is hard-capped at the first apron if it acquires a player in a sign-and-trade. A team that is hard-capped at either apron cannot exceed the apron if the outgoing salary initially leaves it over the apron. A team over the second apron, is not allowed to sign-and-trade a player and receive salary that leaves it over the second apron.

Cash sent: A team is hard-capped at the second apron if cash is sent out in a trade.

Player waived: A team over the first or second apron is not allowed to sign a player during the regular season who was waived and had a preexisting salary greater than the non-tax midlevel exception.

Traded player exception: A team is hard-capped at either if a preexisting trade exception is used. A team is allowed to create a new trade exception and exceed either apron unless it is already hard-capped. For a new trade exception created in a sign-and-trade, a team is not allowed to use it if its post-transaction salary leaves it over the second apron. For example, Denver has a $10.2 million trade exception for Peyton Watson.

Expanded traded player: A trade exception greater than 100% that allows a team to acquire more salary than sent out. A team is hard-capped at the first apron if this exception is used. This applies in a sign-and-trade if salary leaves a team over the second apron.

Trade aggregation: Combining multiple players' salaries in a single trade transaction to acquire a player with a higher salary. This practice is unavailable to teams if the post-transactional salary leaves them over the second apron. A team is also hard-capped at the second apron if aggregating salaries are sent out. For example, Phoenix traded Royce O'Neale and Grayson Allen to Charlotte.

Draft pick freeze: A penalty imposed on teams that exceed the second apron, resulting in a freeze on future first-round draft picks seven years out. For example, if the Denver Nuggets finish over the second apron in 2026-27, then their 2034 first is frozen. If a team finished the 2025-26 season over the second apron, and in at least two of the next four seasons (2026-27 and 2028-29, for example), then its 2033 frozen pick will be moved to the end of the first round, and the team will be unable to trade it.

Unfreezing pick: If the Celtics are in the second apron in 2024-25, but not in 2025-26, 2026-27 and 2027-28 (three out of the four salary cap years), their pick now becomes unfrozen and will not be moved back in the first round.

Post-transaction salary: After a trade or signing, the team's total salary figure must remain under the relevant apron level to avoid additional restrictions.

2026-27 first apron restrictions: Atlanta Hawks (prior trade exception), Boston Celtics (non-tax midlevel), Charlotte Hornets (expanded trade exception), Cleveland Cavaliers (sign-and-trade), Chicago Bulls, Dallas Mavericks (expanded trade exception), Detroit Pistons (non-tax midlevel exception), Indiana Pacers (non-tax midlevel), Los Angeles Lakers (sign-and-trade), LA Clippers (non-tax midlevel), Memphis Grizzlies (non-tax midlevel), Miami Heat (expanded trade exception), Milwaukee Bucks (expanded trade exception), New Orleans Pelicans (non-tax midlevel), Philadelphia 76ers (non-tax midlevel), Portland Trail Blazers (expanded trade exception), Sacramento Kings (biannual), San Antonio Spurs (non-tax midlevel), Toronto Raptors (expanded trade exception), Utah Jazz (non-tax midlevel), Washington Wizards (preexisting trade exception)
2026-27 second apron restrictions: Golden State Warriors (tax midlevel), Houston Rockets (tax midlevel), Minnesota Timberwolves (aggregate trade exception), Phoenix Suns (cash sent)
Not hard-capped at either apron: Brooklyn Nets, Denver Nuggets, New York Knicks, Oklahoma City Thunder, Orlando Magic.

Salary cap exceptions

Full Bird exception: An exception allowing teams to exceed the cap to re-sign players who have been with the team for at least three consecutive seasons. Named after Larry Bird, this helps teams retain critical players. The amount can be up to 25%, 30% or 35% of the cap. The length of a contract is a minimum of one season and the maximum is 5. For example, Austin Reaves signed a four-year $180 million contract with the Lakers using the Bird exception.

Early Bird exception: Allows teams to re-sign players after two years with the team, offering them more than a standard non-Bird exception salary. The exception is 105% of the average player salary or 175% of the previous year's salary. It has a minimum of two and maximum of four years. For example, Gary Trent Jr. signed back-to-back contracts with Milwaukee. He earned early Bird rights and was allowed to sign a four-year, $64 million contract with the Bucks. The contract cannot have a player/team option if two seasons and early Bird apply.

Non-Bird exception: Allows teams to re-sign a player after one year with the team for 120% of their salary from the previous season or 120% of the veteran minimum. It has a maximum of four years. For example, the Clippers re-signed Bradley Beal to a two-year, $13.2 million contract. The first-year salary of $6.4 million was used with the non-Bird exception.

Biannual exception: An exception allowing teams above the cap (but not above the first apron) to sign players every other season. It cannot be used two years in a row. The maximum is two years. The salary is $5.5 million in the first year. The Kings recently signed Precious Achiuwa to the biannual exception.

Disabled player exception: Granted if a player has a season-ending injury. It allows the team to replace the player with a new signing or trade acquisition, up to half of the player's salary for the season, but no more than the non-taxpayer MLE. The maximum is one year.

Offer sheet: A contract offer extended to a restricted free agent by a team other than his original franchise, which has to match the offer to retain the player. The contract has to be for a minimum of two seasons.

Midlevel exception (MLE): Divided into the non-taxpayer, taxpayer, and room midlevel exceptions, MLEs vary based on a team's cap status and provide a way to sign free agents for above the minimum.

Non-taxpayer: Available to teams below the first apron, allowing for longer and higher-value contracts than the taxpayer MLE. It has a minimum of one year and maximum of four years. The salary is $15 million in the first season. If the salary is greater than $6.1 million, the team is hard-capped at the first apron. The Boston Celtics, for example, signed center Mitchell Robinson to the non-tax midlevel exception. They became hard-capped at the first apron as a result.

Taxpayer: Available to teams above the first apron but below the second; has lower limits and is more restrictive in length and value. The value is $6.06 million or less and has a maximum of two years. The Suns recently signed Luke Kennard to the exception.

Veteran minimum: A team may sign a player to, or acquire by assignment, a player contract, not to exceed two seasons in length, that provides for a salary for the first season equal to the minimum player salary applicable to that player (with no bonuses). For a player signing for one season, the two years of service charge applies to the luxury tax and aprons.

Room: For teams that drop below the salary cap (provided they didn't already use one of the other two MLEs), it provides a smaller allowance to add players after using cap space. The salary is $9.4 million, and the maximum years are three. The Los Angeles Lakers signed guard Collin Sexton to the room exception.

First-round rookie scale exception: Governs the salaries of first-round draft picks, setting a pay scale based on draft position. Contracts span four seasons, with team options for Years 3 and 4. The third-year option after the first season can be exercised up until Oct. 31. The fourth-year option after the second season can be exercised up until Oct. 31.

Second-round exception: A player drafted in the second round is allowed to sign either a three- or four-year contract. There is a team option in the last year of the contract.

Standard traded player exception: Generated when a team takes back less or equal salary in return for a traded player. It doesn't trigger a first- or second-apron hard cap, and teams below the apron can pad the outgoing salary by $250,000.

Expanded traded player brackets (ETPE): When a team brings in more salary in return for the outgoing player(s), it uses the ETPE, which triggers a first-apron hard cap. The ETPE has three brackets, which will grow each year proportionately with the salary cap.

First bracket: For up to $8,846,001 in outgoing salary, the team can take back up to 200% plus $250,000.
Second bracket: The outgoing salary of $8,846,000 to $35,384,000 allows for a flat padding of $9.1 million. Recent trade: The Dallas Mavericks acquired Santi Aldama ($17 million) with the expanded traded player exception ($9.1 million) created by the trades of AJ Johnson ($3.2 million) and Khris Middleton ($5.59 million).
Third bracket: If the outgoing salary exceeds $35,384,001, the team can take back up to 125% plus $250,000. Recent trade: The Miami Heat acquired Giannis Antetokounmpo ($58.5 million) using the expanded traded player exception (125% plus $250K) of Tyler Herro ($33 million), Kasparas Jakucionis ($3.8 million), Jaime Jaquez Jr. ($5.9 million) and Kel'el Ware ($4.7 million).

Expiration of trade exceptions: Trade exceptions expire one year after they are created, but additional days are given to prevent expirations occurring on weekends or holidays.

Free agency

Free agent moratorium: Beginning at midnight on July 1 and ending at midnight July 6, the moratorium period is a "holding phase" when teams cannot officially sign free agents or execute trades. Certain transactions are allowed, such as signing rookies and players on minimum deals.

Incomplete roster charge: During the offseason, a team with fewer than 12 players will incur a "roster charge" that fills open spots with placeholder salaries at the rookie minimum (approximately $1.35 million for 2026-27). This prevents teams from dropping players simply to create cap space.

Max salary tiers: The highest percentage of the salary cap a player can earn is based on their years of service (YOS). A player with 0-6 YOS can earn up to 25% of the salary cap, 7-9 YOS up to 30% and 10-plus YOS can earn up to 35%.

Qualifying offer: Players who have finished their rookie scale contract, have three or fewer years of service (but not a first-round pick who had his third- or fourth-year team option), or have finished a two-way contract are eligible to receive a one-year qualifying offer. The offer can be extended from the day after the NBA Finals until June 29. If the offer is extended, the player becomes a restricted free agent.

Restricted free agent (RFA): A player who can sign an offer sheet with any team, but the original team can immediately match it and retain the player.

Arenas provision: The "Gilbert Arenas Rule" prevents a team from offering a first-year salary in an offer sheet that exceeds the non-tax midlevel exception ($15 million in 2026-27) even if they have cap space. A team with cap space could instead backload a multiyear offer with significant raises in the third and fourth years. This scenario played out in 2016, when the Brooklyn Nets signed guard Tyler Johnson to a four-year, $50 million offer sheet -- with $38.4 million backloaded into Years 3 and 4.

Two-way, Exhibit 9, 10 and 10-day deals

Two-way contract eligibility: A player must have fewer than four years of service to be eligible for a two-way contract. Players with four YOS can also sign a two-way contract, but only if they missed one season because of injury.

Maximum games played: The maximum games played on a two-way contract is 50. The number is prorated if a player signs during the regular season.

Maximum two-way contracts: The maximum years for a player to sign with the same team is three. For example, a player is allowed to sign three consecutive two-ways or 2+1 or 1+2.

Two-way contract salary: A two-way contract player's salary is 50% of the minimum player salary for a player with zero years of service. For example, if the veteran minimum is $1.35 million, the two-way contract salary would be $678,882.

Summer contracts: A non-guaranteed one-year contract that does not count against the team's salary cap until the regular season (should the player make the roster). Summer contracts are typically accompanied by Exhibits 9 and 10 and used for players in training camps or with uncertain roster spots.

Extensions

Veteran: The maximum length of an extension is five seasons, including the remaining years left on the original contract. The extension can be signed for players who originally signed a three-, four- or five-year contract. The eligibility to sign is on the second-year anniversary (three- or four-year original contract) or third-year anniversary (five-year original contract). The maximum amount is 140% of the previous year's salary if above the EAP or 140% of the estimated average player salary ($15.1M). The extension cannot exceed the maximum salary allowed in most cases. However, a player is allowed to sign for 105% of the previous season even if the first-year extension exceeds the maximum allowed.

Rookie: A player on a first-round rookie contract is eligible after the third season and up until the last day of the offseason. The maximum is six years, including the remaining season on the original contract, and can be for up to 25% of the salary cap. A player who signs for 25% of the cap is allowed to negotiate escalator clauses for up to 30% of the cap in Year 1. This is based on All-NBA, DPOY and MVP in the current season.

Extend-and-trade: A method where a team extends and trades a player's contract, allowing a longer commitment for the receiving team. The 2023 CBA increased the allowed extension from three to four years and raised the maximum salary increase from 105% to 120% of the first-year salary. Raises are limited to 5%. If a player's extension exceeds the limits of the extend-and- trade, they cannot be traded for six months.

Renegotiation-and-extend: A process that allows teams with cap space to increase a player's salary during the current season and then extend their contract. This approach is helpful for teams with cap space aiming to secure long-term deals for players with two or more years left. The current season is renegotiated (up, never down) and typically includes an extension of up to 140% of the new salary. An extend-and-trade allows for a 40% drop in the subsequent season. Players in recent years (as of 2024-25) to renegotiate-and-extend include Myles Turner, Domantas Sabonis, Jonathan Isaac and Jordan Clarkson.

stories.headline: Every MLB team's chance of signing Skubal -- and their backup plans
stories.summary: Dodger or Met blue? We break down all 30 clubs' chances of landing the offseason's biggest free agent -- and who their Plan B should be.
stories.body:
Tarik Skubal is the golden ticket in the 2026-27 MLB free agent class. In what is viewed as a weak group of free agents, the two-time Cy Young Award winner is the clear difference-maker, a pitcher with a 2.42 ERA over the past three seasons.

The state of modern pitching is at an interesting inflection. While starters are throwing harder than ever -- with even more unhittable breaking balls and a wider variety of pitches -- it is also arguably harder than ever to fill 162 starts in a season, let alone fill enough quality innings. In 2026, 377 different pitchers started a game -- an average of 12.6 per team -- and Michael Wacha was the only pitcher to throw 200 innings.

Ten years ago, there were 310 different pitchers who started a game and 15 pitchers who reached 200 innings. Twenty years ago, those figures were 303 starters and 45 who reached 200 innings. Forty years ago, it was 9.6 starters per team and 52 who pitched 200 innings -- and a total of 82 who pitched 162 innings compared to just 46 in 2026.

You get the idea: An ace starter on Skubal's level is a special addition to any roster. Of course, with Skubal perhaps in line for a $300 million contract, not every team has the same odds of signing him -- although, who knows, a new labor deal could drastically change how these deals unfold.

With that, let's introduce the Skubal Tiers -- breaking all 30 teams into tiers on their likelihood of landing Skubal. And since every team needs pitching help of some sort, we'll include a reasonable backup pitching plan for each team.

Note: References to projected contracts are from Kiley McDaniel's ranking of the top 50 free agents, while references to a team's payroll are drawn from the roster resource section at FanGraphs.

Tier 5: There is absolutely no shot

The teams in this tier are mostly the ones you would expect: the so-called small-market teams with owners unwilling to spend big in free agency (despite San Diego having proved a higher-spending approach is possible). Even a new system with a salary floor is unlikely to change habits overnight, so we'll go straight to the backup pitching plans for these teams.

30. Colorado Rockies

Backup plan: Zac Gallen. It's not that the Rockies never sign free agent starters -- heck, just last year they signed Jose Quintana, Tomoyuki Sugano and Michael Lorenzen -- it's just that they haven't signed a premium free agent starter since Mike Hampton in 2001 (at $121 million, that remains the second-biggest free agent contract in Rockies history). Those veterans last offseason were all signed to one-year deals, so the Rockies are basically in the same situation, looking to fill out a rotation with pitchers that no other team really wants.

29. Athletics

Backup plan: Shota Imanaga. Back in 1993 -- let's see, that was 33 years ago -- the A's re-signed free agents Mark McGwire and Ruben Sierra to identical five-year, $28 million contracts. The 1993 A's proceeded to go 68-94, and maybe that scared them off forever from signing top-tier free agents. Believe it or not, the A's have since signed only two free agents to bigger contracts: Billy Butler for $30 million in 2015 and Luis Severino for $67 million in 2025. That's the long way of saying Skubal is not going to West Sacramento. But Imanaga fits the Severino mold of overpaying for a mid-rotation starter.

28. Cincinnati Reds

Backup plan: Kris Bubic/Dustin May. The Reds need a starter to replace Hunter Greene, who will miss the entire season after Tommy John surgery, but the top 10 highest free agent contracts in franchise history don't even add up to Skubal's projected $352 million contract. To the Reds' credit, they did at least sign Chase Burns to a $105 million extension. They can dip into the less expensive tier of starters like Bubic (projected deal of two years, $18 million) or May (one year, $14 million).

27. Miami Marlins
Backup plan: Raisel Iglesias. Since Bruce Sherman bought the team in 2017, the most the Marlins have paid for a free agent is Jorge Soler's $36 million deal -- so, no, Skubal isn't taking his talents to Little Havana, South Beach, Coral Gables, Key Biscayne, Fort Lauderdale or anywhere else in South Florida. The Marlins were middle of the pack in both rotation ERA and bullpen ERA, but will need a closer to replace Pete Fairbanks, so that's probably a priority over a starter (assuming they don't trade Sandy Alcantara and open up a hole). Iglesias is doable on a one-year, $14 million deal.

26. Kansas City Royals

Backup plan: Chris Bassitt/Kevin Gausman. The Royals dug into the pitching market back in 2024, signing Michael Wacha and Seth Lugo -- and the pair helped them win a wild card that season. Both even later signed extensions, and Wacha was the only pitcher in the majors to reach 200 innings in 2026. The Royals do need rotation help after ranking 25th in ERA, and Bassitt is the kind of low-cost vet they can get on a one-year deal. If they want to get more aggressive, Gausman has better strikeout stuff than Bassitt, and his projected three-year, $51 million deal won't break the payroll.

25. Minnesota Twins

Backup plan: Steven Okert/Jason Adam. To improve on a rotation that ranked 22nd in ERA, the Twins will hope Pablo Lopez is ready after missing all of 2026 due to Tommy John surgery. A rotation with Lopez, Joe Ryan, Taj Bradley, Dean Kremer and the Bailey Ober/Zebby Matthews/Connor Prielipp group has promise and depth. If anything, the Twins might trade one of Ryan, Kremer or Ober, who are all in their final season before free agency. In the meantime, Minnesota's offseason pitching focus will be the bullpen, which it avoided addressing last offseason.

24. Cleveland Guardians

Backup plan: Casey Mize. The Guardians return their five regular starters from 2026, but might still look to upgrade the back of the rotation -- and perhaps look to trade Tanner Bibee. The five-year, $48 million contract Bibee signed a few years ago starts ramping up in cost, as he's due $7.4 million in 2027, $10.4 million in 2028 and $21.4 million in 2029. The Guardians traded infielder Andres Gimenez when his deal reached this point, so a similar decision could be made with Bibee. Mize could be a great add-low move after he struggled the final two months with the Padres.

23. Houston Astros

Backup plan: Nick Martinez/Nick Pivetta. Skubal to the Astros? That would be like signing up for Napoleon's army right before the Battle of Waterloo. If the Astros are going to give $300 million to anyone, it will be with an extension for 2026 AL MVP Yordan Alvarez, not a free agent from another team (the biggest free agent contract since Jim Crane bought the team has been Josh Hader's $95 million deal). That said, the rotation was a mess, finishing 27th in ERA and last in walk rate. New general manager Randy Flores has a tough task to improve this pitching staff, but given the walk problems, adding a strike-thrower like Martinez or Pivetta is the way to go.

Tier 4: It's not likely ... but it sure would be fun

22. Pittsburgh Pirates

The owners' latest salary cap proposal included a salary floor of $180.2 million. The Pirates' payroll currently sits at an estimated $129 million after finishing 2026 at $109 million. So, umm, the Pirates could maybe afford Skubal in a different world than currently exists and can dream of a 1-2 duo of Skubal and Paul Skenes.

Backup plan: David Peterson/Erick Fedde. The rotation has the potential to improve significantly from last year's No. 14 ranking in ERA -- especially Skenes and Bubba Chandler, who had a promising if erratic rookie season. Mitch Keller is coming off a shoulder injury and a 5.29 ERA, but he's signed for two more years, so Pittsburgh isn't going to be eager to push him out. Still, adding a veteran swingman/sixth starter seems prudent.

21. Los Angeles Angels

With Stan Kroenke coming on as the new owner -- the sale won't be officially approved until January -- maybe there will be a new era of Angels baseball where, if Skubal remains unsigned before the lockout, Kroenke comes out and makes an offer Skubal can't refuse. More realistic: Good luck convincing Skubal to sign with a team that hasn't had a winning record since 2015.

Backup plan: High-leverage relievers. The Angels don't have a head of baseball operations yet, with former Cardinals exec John Mozeliak currently in an interim role, so it might be a slow offseason in Anaheim. If they do make any significant pitching moves, it's more likely to be to upgrade a bullpen that ranked 22nd in ERA and 30th in win probability added.

20. Washington Nationals

The Nationals do have plenty of payroll space for a franchise-altering signing, sitting on an estimated $84 million payroll. Maybe Skubal believes they're heading in the right direction. Maybe they are!

Backup plan: Freddy Peralta/Kaima Taira/Trevor Rogers. With so much payroll flexibility and a bad rotation, the Nationals are likely to do something significant and should go after the best of the non-Skubal starters. Peralta (No. 3), Taira (No. 7) and Rogers (No. 10) rank in the top 10 of available free agents and, importantly for the still-building Nationals, will each be 30 or younger on Opening Day.

19. Baltimore Orioles

Maybe Skubal is a big fan of crab cakes and Edgar Allan Poe.

Backup plan: Kevin Gausman/Tyler Mahle/Nick Pivetta. Baltimore's rotation wasn't as bad as perceived -- 17th in ERA, sixth in innings -- but Trevor Rogers and Chris Bassitt are free agents, so the Orioles need at least one replacement (they do have a bunch of prospects in the high minors ready to compete for rotation spots). These three vets fit into a similar projected salary range of three years, $50 million.

18. Atlanta Braves

Skubal plus Chris Sale plus a healthy Spencer Strider would rekindle memories of Greg Maddux, John Smoltz and Tom Glavine.

Backup plan: Sonny Gray. Alas, the Braves just don't do these monster deals in free agency. They've extended several of their own players to nine-figure contracts, but B.J. Upton's $75 million contract in 2013 remains the biggest free agent signing in franchise history. Gray, a Tennessee native, would love to pitch closer to home, and a projected two-year, $42 million deal fits the Braves.

17. San Francisco Giants

The Giants have obviously had trouble luring marquee free agents in recent years, making aggressive pursuits of Bryce Harper, Aaron Judge and Shohei Ohtani since 2019. Coming off a 65-97 season, it won't be easy to lure Skubal to the Bay Area -- and the rotation's problems suggest they may need to spread money around anyway.

Backup plan: Freddy Peralta/Clay Holmes/Michael King/Shota Imanaga. With Logan Webb missing time, not a single Giants starter pitched 162 innings to qualify for the ERA list. The rotation finished 24th in ERA, 25th in strikeout rate and 23rd in walk rate -- and those numbers look even worse after factoring in their home park. Trevor McDonald, Carson Whisenhunt and Blade Tidwell are already out for 2027. With holes to fill, look for the Giants to make a run at those top non-Skubal starters.

16. Texas Rangers

Before the last lockout in 2021-2022, the Rangers made two huge signings right before it began, locking up Corey Seager for $325 million and Marcus Semien for $175 million. Could they make a shocking splash like that again?

Backup plan: Tyler Mahle. President of baseball operations Chris Young recently told local media that the Rangers plan a payroll "very similar" to 2026, which leaves about $20 million to maneuver -- and they need to address the lineup. They could look to flip Seager (which won't be easy, with five years left on his deal at $31.5 million per season), Jacob deGrom (he's making $37 million) or Nathan Eovaldi (making $24 million) to clear some payroll space. Young hinted he's open to some trades -- "there will be changes," he said -- although all three of those players have no-trade protection. The Rangers were 16th in rotation ERA, but just 24th in road ERA. Bringing back Mahle would be an upgrade over Jack Leiter or Kumar Rocker.

Tier 3: Maybe, but they don't really need a starter

15. Milwaukee Brewers

The Brewers' projected payroll sits right about where it was in 2026. Even if there is room to go a little higher following their title, that might go into locking up World Series MVP William Contreras on a long-term deal before he heads to free agency following the 2027 season. In the meantime, while they did make a deal for Dustin May for temporary rotation help down the stretch in 2026, they have depth here with Jacob Misiorowski, Logan Henderson, Robert Gasser, Kyle Harrison, Shane Drohan, Brandon Sproat and the hopeful return of Quinn Priester. Heck, they could even try Aaron Ashby again as a starter, plus Chad Patrick is around as a reliable swingman.

Backup plan: Trade Trevor Megill? Knowing the way the Brewers operate, Megill is a trade possibility as he enters his final season before free agency. With Abner Uribe or Ashby more than capable of stepping in as closer, Megill could be flipped for ... the next Trevor Megill.

14. Seattle Mariners

The rotation has declined from its 2024 performance (3.38 ERA up to 4.05 in 2026), but this was still a group that at least led the majors in innings pitched. Luis Castillo got traded at the deadline with rookie Kade Anderson ready to step in after his late-season audition. Ryan Sloan is another top prospect who could make an impact in the second half. Indeed, the Mariners might look to make a trade here -- Logan Gilbert, with one more year of team control, would be the big ask, with George Kirby and Bryce Miller lesser options.

Backup plan: Bryan Abreu/Pete Fairbanks. The Mariners do need to revamp their bullpen. They're certainly familiar with Abreu, who would give them a power arm from the right side to set up Andres Munoz. Abreu had a terrible first half for the Astros but was back on track in the second half with a 1.71 ERA.

13. Philadelphia Phillies

The Phillies will once again rely on the big three of Cristopher Sanchez, Zack Wheeler and Jesus Luzardo for their playoff hopes, plus Aaron Nola and Andrew Painter. There isn't much depth past those five starters, but president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski must address the lineup (and hopefully improve the defense as well). A right-handed-hitting outfielder tops that list, and there is a hole in the infield with Luis Arraez and Alec Bohm free agents.

Backup plan: Adrian Morejon/Alex Vesia. Alas, the bullpen -- Phillies fans have heard this before -- still needs help behind closer Jhoan Duran. Jose Alvarado's struggles left the Phillies without a reliable lefty in the bullpen, a void Morejon (second in strikeouts among left-handed relievers the past two seasons) or Vesia (fifth) can fill.

12. New York Yankees

With everyone back from a rotation that led the majors in ERA this past season and ranked third in strikeout rate -- Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole, Carlos Rodon, Will Warren and Ryan Weathers, plus Clarke Schmidt, Luis Gil and Elmer Rodriguez as depth -- the Yankees have the top projected rotation for 2027 and have other needs to fill.

Backup plan: Adrian Morejon/re-signing David Bednar and Paul Blackburn. Bringing back Bednar as the closer is a top priority (the Yankees gave him a qualifying offer), with re-signing Blackburn right up there, too, following his big season as Bednar's top setup guy. Finally, adding the power-armed Morejon would be the cherry on top.

11. Boston Red Sox

Even after Sonny Gray opted out of his player option, the Red Sox have a rotation with Garrett Crochet, Ranger Suarez, Payton Tolle, Brayan Bello and Jake Bennett, with Tanner Houck and Johan Oviedo ready to go coming off injuries. Deadline trades depleted more depth -- Connelly Early to the Nationals for Curtis Mead, as well as prospects Anthony Eyanson and Kyson Witherspoon to the Orioles for Adley Rutschman -- but Boston's top offseason priority will focus on the lineup.

Backup plan: Maybe a reliever? Boston's bullpen was actually very good, ranking second in ERA behind the Yankees, and all the key guys will return. But you can never have too many relievers, and the Red Sox had some surprising performers who might not be able to repeat their 2026 numbers.

Tier 2: The long shots

10. Tampa Bay Rays

OK, this is certainly a long shot -- the highest free agent contract the Rays have given was a $40 million deal for Zach Eflin, but imagine a new world with a salary floor. Maybe the Rays operate like they always have, except now they can add one big superstar to the payroll.

Alternatively, they could also trade Drew Rasmussen -- making $20 million in the final year of his contract -- to acquire prospects or younger starters, and then use some of that money to go after Skubal. By the way, Rasmussen's $20 million salary would be the highest single-season salary in franchise history.

Backup plan: Re-sign Nick Martinez. The veteran right-hander needs a good defense behind him given his low strikeout rate, which is why he's a better fit for Tampa Bay than other teams (he went 15-6 with a 3.10 ERA for the Rays in 2026). He turned down his $20 million player option, looking for a multiyear deal, which the Rays should consider giving him.

9. St. Louis Cardinals

The Cardinals never play in this end of the pool -- Matt Holliday is the only $100 million free agent they've signed, and that was a re-signing situation -- but they do have enormous payroll flexibility and a young, up-and-coming roster to sell Skubal on. St. Louis' rotation was 24th in strikeout rate and 26th in batting average allowed, lacking starters with swing-and-miss stuff.

Backup plan: Freddy Peralta/Kaima Taira/Trevor Rogers/Tyler Mahle. In lieu of Skubal, the Cardinals should at least be in on the next group of starters. Taira is a fascinating option coming over from Japan, a 5-foot-8 right-hander who gets ridiculous extension despite his short stature and has a four-seam fastball that sits 94-97 mph with good shape.

8. Arizona Diamondbacks

The Diamondbacks have gone down this road before, making Zack Greinke the highest-paid pitcher with a $206 million deal in 2016 and then signing Corbin Burnes to a $210 million deal two offseasons ago. That deal quickly backfired when Burnes blew out his elbow 11 starts into his Arizona tenure, returning to make just three starts in 2026. With four years still left on Burnes' contract, it seems unlikely the Diamondbacks would give another risky megadeal to a starting pitcher -- but maybe owner Ken Kendrick will sell off his baseball card collection to do it. (Hey, don't scoff: It's valued at $130 million-plus.)

Backup plan: Foster Griffin/re-signing Michael Soroka. This level of starter is more likely what the Diamondbacks will look for to fill the rotation, with Griffin (two years, $30 million) and Soroka (two years, $24 million) offering similar contract projections.

7. Chicago Cubs

Reports surfaced that the Cubs won't be pursuing Skubal. If so, that's somewhat understandable, since they have an entire rotation to fill given all their free agents (Clay Holmes, Matthew Boyd, Kevin Gausman, Shota Imanaga, David Peterson) as well as Cade Horton likely to miss much of 2027 and Ben Brown's return uncertain following neck surgery.

It's worth noting that while the Cubs gave nine-figure deals to Alex Bregman and Dansby Swanson this decade, their biggest free agent deal in team history remains Jason Heyward's $184 million contract from the 2015-16 offseason. Outfielders Seiya Suzuki and Ian Happ are also free agents, complicating the decision-making even if Chicago's payroll currently sits about $115 million below last season.

Backup plan: Freddy Peralta/Trevor Rogers/re-sign Holmes. Of the departing free agents, bringing back Holmes makes the most sense. His ground ball style is a good fit with Nico Hoerner, Bregman and Swanson in the infield. Boyd could be a cheaper alternative, while it might be time to move on from the homer-prone Imanaga. What the Cubs have lacked is a power pitcher to headline a rotation. Hmm, maybe there is room for Skubal and another starter.

6. Detroit Tigers

Why not? The Tigers' luxury tax payroll sits at $192 million compared to 2026's total of $230 million. Sure, Skubal would push the total past that, but not over any potential salary cap, and the roster is otherwise pretty set. Factor in that the two highest-paid players on the roster are Framber Valdez, who is signed for just two more seasons, and Javier Baez, whose deal finally runs out after 2027. That gives the Tigers payroll flexibility into the future -- and can entice Skubal to return to Detroit with a roster that already has a young foundation with Kevin McGonigle and Max Clark, plus other top-100 prospects on the way.

Backup plan: Emilio Pagan? Detroit's bullpen had problems, ranking 12th in ERA but 26th in win probability added -- so, that could be the entire focus with the front office comfortable enough with a rotation featuring Valdez, Troy Melton, Keider Montero, Jackson Jobe and River Ryan. Pagan, the Reds' closer the past two seasons, has agreed to a one-year, $11 million deal with the Tigers, but he's hardly a sure bet to be a step up from Kenley Jansen, so another move or two here makes sense.

5. Chicago White Sox

Why not? Chicago is young, fun, exciting and needs an ace. Like the Cardinals, the White Sox have plenty of payroll space and no guaranteed money on the docket beyond 2027. They'd have to convince Skubal that the club's 2026 success was just the first step to a brighter future -- and convince owner Jerry Reinsdorf to offer Skubal a deal he can't refuse. That might be the hard part: Andrew Benintendi's ill-advised $75 million deal a few years ago is the largest free agent contract in White Sox history.

Backup plan: Freddy Peralta/Trevor Rogers/Clay Holmes/Nick Pivetta. OK, Jeff Passan says the White Sox won't be in on Skubal, even though "they absolutely should be." Agreed. Anyway, even though they announced Grant Taylor will be moving to the rotation, they should still be in on the other top starters. Then, the White Sox will need to replace Taylor's valuable innings in the bullpen, so they should be in on all the top relievers as well.

Tier 1: The favorites

4. Toronto Blue Jays

The Blue Jays went big after Shohei Ohtani. They went after Juan Soto. It wouldn't be shocking then, even though they finished last in the majors in runs scored, to see them go after Skubal. The Jays were middle of the pack (15th) in rotation ERA but just 28th in innings pitched, and while they added Jose Soriano at the trade deadline and will be counting on Cody Ponce returning from his ACL injury, Skubal and Dylan Cease would make for a dynamic duo.

Plus, this isn't the best offseason to be adding offense anyway, so maybe the Jays go all-in on a dominant pitching staff.

Backup plan: Kevin Gausman. On the other hand, with Vladimir Guerrero Jr. entering the second year of his $500 million contract and coming off a nine-homer, 57-RBI season, the Jays might find it too risky to have both Guerrero and a $300 million-plus pitcher on the roster. Gausman enjoyed his time in Toronto and could return on a projected three-year, $51 million deal.

3. San Diego Padres

The Padres are viewed as the big wild card in the Skubal sweepstakes. They have an entire rotation in free agency -- Michael King, Walker Buehler, Nick Pivetta, Robbie Ray, Casey Mize, Lucas Giolito -- so will have to do some heavy lifting to plug all the gaps. "We're all-in," new owners Kwanza Jones and Jose E. Feliciano said at their introductory news conference in August.

Will that translate into a megadeal for Skubal? Given the complications of the Manny Machado and Xander Bogaerts contracts, which run through 2033 for two players on the downturn of their careers, the need to win now is glaringly acute. The potential decline of the team in a couple of years, however, could make Skubal wary about signing here.

Backup plan: Re-signing King. It's been a good match the past three seasons and King's projected deal -- three years, $79.5 million -- is a quarter of Skubal's projection for a pitcher who nearly matched Skubal in WAR in 2026. Indeed, the holes in the rotation will require multiple signings, so maybe the rational move is spreading the Skubal money to two or three pitchers.

2. New York Mets

As with Soto a couple of years ago, if owner Steve Cohen wants someone, money won't be the issue. The Mets were 23rd in rotation ERA in 2026, with little certainty for 2027 beyond Nolan McLean and Christian Scott. President of baseball operations David Stearns isn't a fan of long-term pitching contracts, but the Mets will throw all logic aside in trying to turn things around after a losing season. The payroll will take a big drop after 2027, when Sean Manaea ($25 million), Jorge Polanco ($23 million) and Kodai Senga ($14 million) come off the books.

As Passan pointed out, "Even if a salary cap is in place after the upcoming collective bargaining negotiations reach their conclusion, the Mets can sign Skubal and remain under the cap. They'd be top-heavy, sure, but with money to offload to teams that would need to reach a floor."

Backup plan: Nick Martinez/Michael King/Trevor Rogers. Martinez is the opposite of Skubal -- a finesse right-hander -- but he's a good clubhouse guy, which the Mets need after some of the issues this past season, and proved he can handle a starter's workload after pitching 180 innings for the Rays in 2026. Martinez can be had on a reasonable two-year deal that wouldn't blow up the payroll, perhaps allowing the Mets to bring in a second free agent starter like King or Rogers.

1. Los Angeles Dodgers

As Alden Gonzalez reported, Skubal loved his time with the Dodgers, becoming best buddies with Blake Snell along the way and appreciating a veteran clubhouse dedicated to trying to win a World Series. "Incredible organization, incredible teammates, incredible fanbase," Skubal said after the Dodgers were eliminated in the NLCS. "Honored to wear the L.A. across your chest and on the hat."

Yes, the Dodgers' estimated luxury tax payroll already sits at $386 million for 2027 and a potential salary cap would require some tricky roster machinations down the road -- depending on how a cap might be rolled out -- but this is the Dodgers. Right now, nothing prevents them from spending as much money as necessary to re-sign Skubal.

In the short term, they would love to trade Teoscar Hernandez (making $22.1 million in 2027), not just to clear payroll space but to open up an outfield spot for Josue De Paula. Freddie Freeman is a free agent after 2027, and Tyler Glasnow, Edwin Diaz, Tanner Scott and Max Muncy are after 2028, so there is some potential flexibility to re-sign Skubal -- although Kyle Tucker's contract through 2029 will be a big drag in a salary cap world.

Backup plan: Adrian Morejon. Do the Dodgers really need a starter? Not really. With Shohei Ohtani returning to the mound for 2027, they still have him, Snell, Glasnow, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Roki Sasaki, Justin Wrobleski and Emmet Sheehan. Alex Vesia and Evan Phillips are free agents, however, so even though they already have two of the highest-paid relievers in Diaz and Scott, adding one of the best bullpen arms in the game is a potential Plan B.

stories.headline: As Nike replaces Adidas, is UEFA Champions League star ball on its way out?
stories.summary: Nike will replace Adidas as supplier of UEFA Champions League match balls from next season. Will the famous 'star ball' design soon be no more?
stories.body:
Editor's note: This article was first published on Aug. 26, 2026 and has been updated

The UEFA Champions League and UEFA Women's Champions League match balls will boast a brand new look starting next season after UEFA confirmed on Monday that Nike will be taking over from long-standing provider Adidas as the official supplier for the 2027-28 campaign onwards.

Nike will take the reins for the 2027-28 campaign onward after agreeing a deal to supply the official match balls for all three UEFA club competitions from 2027 to 2031 -- the Champions League, the Europa League and the Conference League. According to The Guardian, that deal is worth around $45 million a year, double the value of the final contract with Adidas.

- Man United, Pochettino's to-do list based on what's gone wrong

- Meet Como's Paz, the heir to Messi's Argentina No. 10 shirt

- Champions League talking points: Are Como the real deal?

With Adidas having supplied the official Champions League match ball since 2001, the "star ball" design has become an emblem of the competition. However, the last we see of the iconic pattern might be in the 2026-27 final.

That's because, as things stand, there are no specific details available as to the designs that Nike has in store. In a statement on Monday, UEFA would only say: "Further details on the match ball designs will be revealed in due course." It is also unclear -- and highly unlikely -- that the American sportswear giant will continue with the star theme popularised by Adidas over the past 25 years, as the German powerhouse reportedly hold the rights to the star ball design.

Nike's designs are therefore likely to be fresh and distinct with the intent of drawing a line under Adidas' tenure as UEFA match ball suppliers while also launching their own, modernised visual identity.

Back in August, Adidas unveiled what will be their final iteration of the "star ball," the preliminary eye-catching colourway of which is currently being used throughout the group phase of the 2026-27 Champions League.

The men's version of the 2026-27 Champions League ball is plastered in a neon-spattered livery that, according to Adidas, has been inspired by players creating colourful moments of magic and personal expression while plugging away at training on cold, foggy training pitches during their quest to attain Champions League greatness.

The design for the women's match ball is a little less abstract. The golden-orange pattern takes its inspiration from the aura of the ring of 11 stars that make up the UWCL emblem, with flashes of metallic purple and silver then adding a dash of visual contrast to the mix.

Both balls are based on the template that Adidas have used for their Champions League match balls since the introduction of the "Finale 1" ball for the 2001-02 season. Since then, over 50 iterations of the UCL star ball have been deployed in the competition -- and that's not including the various hi-vis yellow variants that have been used in winter months over the years.

stories.headline: Sources: San Jose Earthquakes sold for $625 million to Heath Freeman
stories.summary: Alden Global Capital co-founder Heath Freeman is purchasing the San Jose Earthquakes from John Fisher, following MLS owners' approval of the sale Thursday.
stories.body:
The San Jose Earthquakes announced that Alden Global Capital co-founder Heath Freeman will acquire the team, as well as the club's home venue, PayPal Park, from John Fisher.

Sources confirmed a report from Sportico that the sale reflects an enterprise value of $625 million. The MLS board of governors unanimously approved the transfer of ownership Thursday, noting that the transaction will close in the coming weeks.

The deal will complete a lengthy sales process that began in June 2025. Investment bank Moelis helped facilitate the deal.

"My family and I are honored and humbled to be the next generation owners of the San Jose Earthquakes. I would like to thank John Fisher and the Fisher family for their confidence in me. I know how much they love this team and we expect to continue making them proud in this new era of the Quakes," Freeman said.

"Our vision is simple - winning on and off the field for San Jose and the entire region. The Bay Area is home to some of the world's great institutions, sports franchises and leaders. The standard has been set. We are eager to partner with and connect our community more closely with the Earthquakes and immerse them in our world."

The Quakes struggled during much of Fisher's tenure as owner, reaching the postseason just four times in the past 11 seasons. This season, under manager Bruce Arena, San Jose is in the MLS Cup Playoffs. It will face Houston Dynamo FC in Round 1 when it hosts Game 1 of the best-of-three series Nov. 24 at PayPal Park. The club won the 2012 Supporters' Shield.

"We are committed to investing in the team and building a club that consistently competes for championships," Freeman said. "Off the field, we are equally focused on strengthening our connections with fans and communities in San Jose and throughout the Bay Area. We believe the future of the Earthquakes is incredibly bright, and we can't wait to get started and take the Quakes to unforeseen heights."

Freeman has served as president of Alden Global Capital since 2014. He currently serves as chairman of Tribune Enterprises LLC, which owns and manages newspapers including the Chicago Tribune and South Florida Sun Sentinel, and as vice chairman of MNG Enterprises Inc., which manages newspapers such as The Denver Post, the Mercury News and the Boston Herald. Alden Global Capital has recently enacted deep cost cuts across its publications, leading to multiple layoffs.

Fisher has owned the Earthquakes since 2007, when he and Lew Wolff purchased an expansion team to replace the side that relocated to Houston after the 2005 season. During his tenure, he privately financed the construction of PayPal Park.

"My family and I have loved owning this club for almost 20 years and we are extremely grateful for the support of our amazing fans as well as the hard work of all of our coaches, players and staff," Fisher said. "We would like to thank Jared Shawlee and the executive staff for their leadership and the entire Quakes front office for their commitment to the club, the fans and the community."

"I want to thank John Fisher and his family for their nearly two decades of commitment to the San Jose Earthquakes, Major League Soccer and the Bay Area soccer community," said MLS commissioner Don Garber.

"John has been a great partner and a good friend, and his leadership and investment helped build a strong foundation for the club. Heath Freeman is an ambitious owner with a strong belief in the Earthquakes and the Bay Area as one of the country's great soccer markets. We are excited to welcome him to MLS and look forward to the energy and vision he will bring to this next chapter of the club."

Two MLS teams remain on the market. The Saputo family announced plans to sell CF Montréal earlier this week. The Vancouver Whitecaps are also still on the market, with Goldman Sachs leading that process.

BMO Capital Markets is managing the CF Montréal sale as lead financial adviser, with National Bank of Canada Capital Markets as co-adviser.

stories.headline: Ciryl Gane survives early onslaught, edges Josh Hokit in UFC 334 main event
stories.summary: Ciryl Gane got all he could handle from Josh Hokit in a five-round slugfest but took command late to defend his heavyweight title at UFC 334.
stories.body:
NEW YORK -- In the end, Josh Hokit proved to be more than just a shtick.

Ciryl Gane defended his UFC heavyweight championship Saturday by outlasting Hokit in a spirited five-round main event at UFC 334 at Madison Square Garden. All three judges scored the bout 48-47 for Gane in his second title defense; he previously scored a second-round stoppage over Alex Pereira in June at the White House.

Despite Gane (15-2) getting the decision, Hokit (10-1) might have won the night. Hokit, 29, was a relative unknown when he joined the UFC just 15 months ago, but he has quickly built his name around controversial -- at times, ugly -- trash talk.

On Saturday, however, he showed that there is plenty of substance behind the persona. He pushed Gane backward with relentless pressure and won over the New York crowd with his durability and willingness to press forward.

"I will rejoice in my suffering," Hokit said in his postfight Octagon interview. "Suffering builds endurance. Endurance builds character. Character builds hope. I will never lose hope. I will be champion one day. You guys can kick me when I'm down, I'll still break your f---ing leg."

Gane, whose only losses have come against Jon Jones and Francis Ngannou, credited Hokit's approach and said he expected a challenge Saturday despite oddsmakers listing him as a clear favorite.

"All the people around the world [took him lightly], but not me," Gane said. "This guy is a motherf---er. He did very well."

According to UFC Stats, Gane outlanded Hokit 298-243 in total strikes, and their 541 combined strikes set a record for a heavyweight bout. Gane's 237 significant strikes also broke the UFC heavyweight record.

Much of that volume could be attributed to Hokit's game plan. He ran at Gane from the opening bell and set a frantic pace of striking and grappling exchanges. Gane did well to disrupt his pressure with jabs and body punches, but Hokit weathered the shots well. He electrified the New York crowd with a huge slam at the end of the first round and appeared to hold momentum through the second and third rounds.

"There's no doubt that Hokit's stock goes up, even with me," UFC CEO Dana White said. "I thought this guy was a bigmouthed goofball, and I hated his shtick and the whole thing. I respect the s--- out of that guy. He is the real deal."

Gane's championship background showed in the final two rounds. He continued to land knees and punches to the body and took control of the striking exchanges in the final round.

The win could set up potential rematches for Gane against Pereira, former champion Tom Aspinall and Alexander Volkov, as well as a new matchup against Russian knockout artist Sergei Pavlovich.

stories.headline: How Kimi Antonelli overcame George Russell, Ferrari to become F1's youngest champion
stories.summary: How Kimi Antonelli overcame early setbacks, teammate George Russell and a Ferrari fightback to become Formula 1's youngest-ever world champion.
stories.body:
Kimi Antonelli was crowned the 2026 Formula 1 world champion at the Mexico City Grand Prix, sealing the title with four races of the season remaining.

He stood on the last step of the podium, behind race winner Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton in the Ferrari.

At 20 years old, Antonelli made his title fight look remarkably easy. He laid down the foundations with his maiden victory at the second race of the season in China, and with the exception of the occasional reliability setback with his Mercedes, he remained composed ever since.

It marked Mercedes' return to the top winning its first drivers' and constructors' trophy since Hamilton six years ago, and the team have well and truly unlocked their next superstar -- a superstar simply just enjoying himself.

Here are the highs -- and few low points -- that shaped his title-winning campaign.
